Let's get started with a quick overview of three-statement modeling tests and why banks and other finance firms give you them. The idea here is that you take a
[02:44] company's historical income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement, and then you project them over usually a 5-year period. So, in this case, for this company, Otis, we would go to their 10-K, and we would go down to where they have the financial statements and supplementary data, and then we would either go through the PDF format of this and copy and paste it in from here, which is not very efficient, or we would bring up the Excel or CSV version and use that one, and we would paste in these financials, and then we'd create projections to see what they look like over the next 5 years, from 2022 to 2026. You do this because you want to
[03:19] determine whether the company's projected growth and margins and free cash flow and other metrics are actually realistic. For example, maybe the company says something like, "We'll generate $5 of free cash flow, and then use it to repay $1 of debt, and then return $4 to shareholders in the form of dividends and share repurchases." If you build a proper three-statement model, you can assess whether that's realistic, whether the company might actually need outside funding, whether it's not in fact going to generate this much in free cash flow, and you also can tell what happens if market conditions
[03:51] change or if the company's business takes a turn for the worse, for example. Now, in terms of the types of three-statement modeling tests, the first category here is when you have a blank sheet and a strict time limit, like 30 minutes, 60 minutes, 90 minutes, 2 hours, maybe even up to 3 or 4 hours. These tests are more about working quickly, knowing Excel shortcuts very, very well, simplifying, and then making quick decisions under pressure and not overthinking what to do. Now, another category here is when you have a template and also a strict time
[04:24] limit. So, they might give you a partially complete version that has all the data filled in, but then you have to make the projections. In this case, it's more about entering the correct formulas, justifying your assumptions, and then you often have to answer questions based on the model's output here because you don't have to do all the data entry, which sometimes frees up 30 minutes, 40 minutes, even 60 minutes. And then the last category is when there is no strict time limit. So, maybe you have a couple days or a week, but you're not talking about 60 minutes or 2 hours. In this case, it's much more about doing some outside research and using the data
[04:58] to justify your assumptions for the revenue, expense, and cash flow projections. You will often make some type of presentation at the end. So, you're not necessarily just answering questions, you're actually making a presentation to the firm or the group you're interviewing with at the end as well. [26:11] the historical test year looking at rate base more closely rate bases the reasonable and prudent cost of property on which the public utility is authorized to earn its rate of return you determine what the race rate base is by taking the original cost of the utility assets assuming that they were prudent capital investments and subtract accumulate accumulated depreciation expense so what is the original cost the

[00:00] hey guys welcome back to another video today we're going to be talking about calculating normalized ebitda when selling your private company in an m a transaction and so this video is both for sellers that are looking to learn about what ebada is and what can be normalized and what can't be normalized and it's also for buyers to understand when you're looking at a cim or a document prepared by a seller to really look at certain areas and understand is this a fair ebitda addback yes or no so just to start off we'll provide a
[00:35] quick background so earnings before interest tax depreciation and amortization or ebitda is a financial metric referring to the profit generated by the business prior to any financial and accounting adjustments this metric is used to source financing from banks or investors and is used by most entrepreneurs when buying and valuing a business now typically when we talk about buying companies a lot of the times in the private lower mid market space and even with small businesses you'll say it's an
[01:08] ebidell multiple it's a multiple four times it's a multiple of seven times whatever the case is depending on the sector you're multiplying the ebitda of the company by a certain number and that's what gives you the value of the company so a million dollars times a multiple four is four million dollars in enterprise value the value of the business but when you're selling your business you actually normalize the ipad to determine the true value of the company because the ebitda on the financial statements may not be truly reflective of what the potential ebitda is for a new buyer because owners may
[01:42] run expenses through the business that would reduce their taxable income and it's effective for them personally but when they go to sell their business they want to really remove those discretionary non-essential non-recurring costs out of the business by normalizing them so that's when whenever you hear the word normalize it means to back out these personal discretionary expenses now some people are going to be aggressively normalizing and so you need to be pretty fair and even keeled in terms of how you approach what is a true normalization versus what
[02:14] isn't and that's what i'm gonna be talking about in this video but at the basic core the financial version of calculating ebitda before any normalizations is fairly easy it's in the name interest tax depreciation and amortization so you always start with the bottom at the bottom of the income statement you start with your net income you then add back the income taxes that are paid you add back any depreciation and amortization which in this instance is 235 000 and then you add back interest on debt
[02:48] and what you're adding back interest on debt is only on the long-term third-party debt or any shareholder loans where you're paying yourself through interest but the key clarification here and i see this very often is that some people will add back interest on the operating line or bank charges or credit card fees and etc etc and the reality is if if that's required to sustain the day-to-day operating business in terms of working capital in terms of processing credit card fees you know then what changes when you sell the business in terms of
[03:22] customers buying from you well nothing really you're still going to need to use that operating line you're still going to need to process those credit card fees because customers are buying from you so it's unfair and it's not typically seen in the higher end of the lower mid market where you add back operating line interest and credit card fees what you add back is the long-term debt because long-term debt is a decision made by the owner to carry carry debt on the books and you know the new buyer is may not want to put debt on the books may want to completely sell fund the business so you look at what
[03:56] available cash flow is and realistically the cash flow tied up in supporting working capital credit card fees and bank charges is required anyways and regardless of the owner would be incurred so that's not added back so that's a key thing to realize but interest on long-term debt is now if you look back here's really the calculation you take your net income add the interest on long-term debt amortization income taxes and you get your ebitda of 1.789 million dollars now this is not the ebitda that you value a
[04:29] company on because we haven't done the normalizations yet so let's go into the normalizations and before we do that i'd rather just quickly explain for people once again what a normalization is and why it happens and at its core it's the reason why people incur expenses through the business rather than paying themselves and incurring that same personal expense outside of the business is all related to taxes and you know to really simplify it you know say for example you want to pay a personal expense you want to buy a
[05:01] hundred hundred dollars worth of gas for the family camper van to go on a trip it's not a business expense it's your expense do you incur it on the personal credit card or do you put it on the business credit card well if you incur it on the personal business card then you have to first pay yourself a hundred dollars and incur the tax of paying yourself that hundred dollars so really you're paying yourself maybe 126 dollars you pay the tax and then that hundred dollars is used to pay the expense or you pay a hundred dollars using the business's credit card which reduces the taxes paid
[05:35] in the business and it saves you the taxes that you would have paid by paying yourself from the company to you personally so it's always more efficient to incur personal expenses in the company and and obviously not in publicly traded companies where there's scrutiny but in private businesses there's a lot less scrutiny so owners are very frequently incurring expenses that may not be really required by the business so that's why normalizations occur and there are a few common areas where these normalizations are seen the first one
[06:06] and i would say the most common one is owner salaries there's always a normalization when it comes to owner salaries or i would say nine times out of ten and any other family members on the payroll so that's a very common one that will go into an example and look at another one is owner benefits you know personal vehicles so i'm leasing an audi or a cadillac through the business that is not really required to deliver the services of the business it's not a business vehicle my employees don't use it i use it personally and i want to keep it after i sell the business well that's a personal vehicle it's not going
[06:38] to come with the business so you add back the lease costs or the taxes that were incurred to really buy that company that vehicle in the company you know travel expenses with family meals and entertainment golf memberships uh insurance costs on life insurance you know if you say for example your wealth advisor tells you hey listen for your personal planning sake you need to carry a life insurance policy and you use the company to pay for that life insurance policy well again does the buyer really need that life insurance
[07:10] policy probably not it's up to them to decide so it's a discretionary expense that you're incurring using the company's funds and that would be added back as well now another very common thing we see is rent normalization so whether it's rent paid to the owner of the real estate being you as the owner of the business as well and so that's an inter-company rent or it can be rent that you're paying to a landlord that's going to change in the near future that needs to be normalized so that's another very common one then there's one-time costs and again as you can see
[07:43] one-time costs are more you know really non-recurring so it could be a lawyer fee for a big settlement penalties uh foreign exchange losses fines levied on the business by the trade board whatever the case is and it's it's really only paid once it's not expected to be paid again and therefore you know it doesn't really reflect reflect the true expenses of the business moving forward on the opposite end subsidies or non-recurring income and especially with kovid we've found that a lot of sellers
[08:15] believe that they can take the grant and subsidy money that you know the governments have given them to support their employee payroll and their rent subsidies and everything and consider that towards profit when selling their business but that's completely not true like that will not continue moving forward you know a buyer is buying a business using the historical cash flow as a proxy and an estimate of what the future cash flow for them as the new owner will be now when you look at historical levels you want to make sure that you're representing the true recurring sustainable cash flow of the
[08:48] business and the coveted subsidy is not one of them you know it may happen for one or two years at most but you know if an owner's looking at owning this business for 10 years if there's subsidies that are going to be paid for 10 years then totally fine you can add that back and keep it in there but if it's a one one or two year subsidy and it's going to go away then why should the owner pay for that you know he or she is not going to benefit from that income moving forward so that's typically added back and same thing with subsidies around taxes and we'll talk about that as well now one-time profits anything disposal
[09:22] on equipment right so you know say for example you you trade in your piece of equipment and you buy a new piece of equipment and the trade-in value obviously is is much higher than the book value the of the piece of equipment on your balance sheet and then obviously your accountant needs to book again on that sale of the equipment and that drives up your annual profit by fifty thousand dollars well obviously that's non-recurring you know you only have a set finite amount of equipment and you've you've taken that money you've already and already reinvested it in a new piece of equipment so that's not real
[09:54] income that can be made available to investor moving forward so one-time gains on equipment or assets or investments that after they you know gain after selling and exiting that investment that's not considered business income that can be used to value a company and then the last thing and this is really contentious usually and i'll give you a few examples is synergies you know whether it's historical employee synergies or where i've you know shut down a division and and i've added back the cost of those employees because well technically those things are not being
[10:26] incurred now that i've shut down the division so there's a lot of these kind of synergies that would maybe ebitda had backs or they may not be ebitda back so we'll talk about that as well so let's go into the most common one so owners either pay themselves way too little or way too much which skews the unadjusted profit of the business usually when you're looking at just the pure financial statements of the company so when you're preparing your ebitda you need to normalize for owner's salaries back to market levels so i just wanted to define market salary
[11:00] so the market salary is the equivalent salary level associated with the responsibilities performed by that owner in the business so typically when an owner works they will do you know they'll focus on strategy financial reporting they might do some customer relationship management but some owners are very involved in their company and work 90 hours a week and other owners only work 20 hours a week because they're really good at delegating work and so they don't really need to work a full-time role so you want to match
[11:33] whatever they're doing within the business to what it would cost to replace them if you have to go to market tomorrow and hire employees to take over those responsibilities so say for example an owner works 100 hours a week and does the role of three people well now if they sell that business you know the buyer's gonna look at that and say hold on a second i'm not gonna be working 100 hours because i'm not crazy enough like you but i'm gonna need to hire someone to take over those responsibilities so realistically i need to factor in two additional salaries on top of mine when i'm looking at
[12:05] really what the true ebitda is to me as the buyer when i'm looking at your business but that's really case by case so really it's always important when you're talking about owner salary normalizations you're putting yourself in in the buyer's shoes is to say how much would it cost to replace me if i had to hire someone to do the job that i'm doing today and on average i would say for a ceo salary it's anywhere from about a hundred to two hundred thousand dollars that's the normalizing salary against your salary
[12:37] now most owners fail to understand that when investors are buying their business they need to pay themselves a management fee or hire a manager to run that business and incur that salary so in most instances when owners think about oh well i'm not paying myself for salary today and whatever the profit is on the books is the profit of the business no no no that's not ebitda that's seller discretionary earnings that's when you're you're not accounting for any salary normalization when when you're accounting for salary normalizations you have to look at how
[13:09] many hours of you know a week you're working in the business what you're performing and what it would cost to replace you and then you take your historical salary you add that back to profit and then you deduct the cost of replacing you based on your research which may be 100 200 000 and in some instances it can be 500 000 if the person is doing the role of five people right so let's look at an example so jim owns a commercial roofing business and historically pays himself through dividends doesn't collect any salary what he does in the business is he

[00:39] the proportion of senior to subordinate debt principal Reserve fixed versus floating rate fees Etc the theory behind this model is from Keith Allman's 2007 book modeling structured Finance cash flows now because the book is 15 years old these strategies almond takes to build certain components of the rmbs model are a little outdated I think that's due to the fact that XL formulas were not nearly as developed 15 years ago some formulas just didn't exist in addition his model doesn't accrue unpaid interest instead it just
[01:13] marks unpaid interest down as a loss period by period I thought the model would be much more robust if interests were accrued so I built in the accrual into my model in this structured Finance series I'll walk through how the model works and how I built it including accruing interest and also touch on some of the more complex aspects of the model were the ones that gave me the most difficulty for example different interest rate limitations caps floors frequencies which I will touch on likely in the next video then I'll wrap up by displaying
[01:46] how the inputs work what you can see here is what I call the control panel which is made up of three distinct components inputs which are mostly Dynamic and color coded with blue text and static inputs which are color coded as black the second component is the cash flow snapshot which allows the user to peer into the model without actually scrolling through the waterfall or the amortization worksheet when I was building the model I would have to move to say period 200 and then to period 100 and then period 150 and you just lose a
[02:21] lot of time that way so the cash flow snapshot is purely for user efficiency and the third component is a series of tests to ensure that the model is working right the first is a cash in equals Cash Out test ensuring that every single dollar generated by the underlying assets less fees is distributed to the pool that is easily the most complex and difficult test to complete but without it the model can't be said to be accurate the next three tests check balances at maturity the second asset balance ensures the amortization schedule is working right
[02:54] now if the next two tests don't work that is if the senior and subordinate balances don't equal zero at maturity that doesn't mean that the model is inaccurate what it means is that the rate used to generate asset level cash flows isn't high enough to pay off those liabilities which can happen for an array of reasons as you'll soon see I also added this goal seek functionality to solve for a weighted average fixed rate which sets the subordinate tranche in the final period in this case that's the 30 years or 360 months equal to zero and that also ensures that the asset
[03:28] pool generates the exact amount of Revenue to pay off both the senior and subordinate debt the model can switch between four different payment frequencies monthly quarterly semi-annually and annually the way that works is through the dynamic dates and day adjustment if we change the inputs from monthly to quarterly the day adjustment increases to 0.25 and the dates adjust accordingly it's a very efficient way of changing payment frequencies without messing up the model you may have noticed that when I change to a quarterly payment the subordinate
[04:00] principle doesn't get paid off and the balance of maturity is negative 20 million that's because the fixed rate which is set to pay off the subordinate debt um was calculated with monthly payments with less frequent payments principal is unable to get paid off as quickly and therefore a higher rate is going to be required this is a great time to see how the goal seek functionality works and explore the effect frequency can have on the liability structure so let me solve for the rate which sets the final subordinate liability balance
[04:32] equal to zero that's an interesting part of this model I forgot about there's so many permutations here that even my new laptop is having a hard time solving for that fixed rate so I'm going to help the goal seek out a little and get the number closer to zero and then solve with goseek again now you can see that the interest rate
[05:09] required to pay off the subordinate tranche has increased by about 100 basis points meaning that the jump from monthly to quarterly payments has quite a large impact on the sequential payment structure moving on to the amortization worksheet
[05:42] which is actually the heart of the model it's built in two stages the inertial amortization tables textbook paying down principal as the difference between notional payment and required interest the trickiest part here is to have interest rates reflect the confines of the inputs such as interest rate caps and Floors like I mentioned previously to the right is actual amortization in effect the pool principle is reduced by defaults prepayments and amortizations defaults are not paid out as cash flow
[06:15] though they only decrease the total balance Omen also includes a basic credit swap so I include one as well I'm not going to touch on the credit swap because it's not the focus of the model and really doesn't make much of a difference now for the waterfall the most complex part of the model this is the first structured Finance model I've ever built so I admit that the model could be much cleaner and have more robust assumptions and there is one key item to note here the model I built pays off interest and principles sequentially meaning that the
[06:48] senior tranche is paid interest then the senior tranche is paid to principal then the subordinate tranche is paid interest and then the subordinate tranches paid principle I know that in many cmbs models tranche interest is paid to each tranche sequentially then principle is paid sequentially with interest shortfalls being applied first to interest then to principal cash flows from the modified amortization table come in here at column I and then fees are subtracted as I noted I built the waterfall to pay off senior interest senior principal
[07:20] subordinate interest and finally subordinate principal so in effect although there's only two tranches there are four waterfalls in this model unpaid interest is accrued but unpaid principle is counted as a loss that being said the model doesn't count for that and I saw for zero principal loss with the goal seek function I'll show you how the interest works here in columns M through Q interest is calculated accrued if not paid off in the previous period and then paid off
[07:54] with the cash flow available for distribution this interest tracker here zeros out when all unpaid interest has been settled a negative number in the tracker means that the interest balance is being paid down whereas a positive number means that the interest balance is growing cash remaining column R is simply the difference between cash flow available for distribution and the interest paid to the senior tranche which concludes the first waterfall from the available cash flow after senior interest pool senior principal is paid off there's also a working principal Reserve which
[08:27] you can see here in columns a b through AE which is funded by a set amount every month the remaining cash flow in column W includes that principal Reserve skipping over to the subordinate structure note interest do is calculated the same way as in the senior debt structure the only difference here is that interest paid is based off cash flow remaining after paying off the senior interest in principal then principal paid is the minimum of either cash flow remaining after senior
[09:00] interest senior principal and support an interest or the principal due okay if all goes well we've paid off our liabilities but what happens if there's extra cash flow well the model is currently set to not generate a lot of extra cash flow since her liabilities are set to pay off exactly at the end of the period but if I increase the weighted average fixed rate we can see what happens so I'm just going to increase that fixed rate to seven percent now excess cash flow is calculated as
[09:33] the difference between cash remaining after the senior tranche and total subordinate interest due that's a bit of a shortcut and wouldn't work for multiple tranches but with two tranches it works for two reasons first because of the assumption that senior interests and principles paid before subordinate interest then subordinate principal and second because in that case all excess cash flow is applied to the senior tranche and then all access cash flow is applied to the subornet tranche there's only one case where excess principle is split between the
[10:07] two and that's when the senior tranche is paid off and the subordinate tranche starts to get paid off we can see here in row 217 that the same structure applies to the subordinate tranche right if principle was left over after paying the senior tranche it flows through to subordinate debt like I mentioned and that's pretty much how this basic rmbs model works like I said it's a very basic model with simplistic waterfall assumptions and the model itself is not very robust but as you'll see next video it's a good way to test

[B] PE Fund Performance Metrics: TVPI vs. MOIC vs. DPI and Gross vs. Net IRR
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bGhv_Kox5RA
channel: Mergers & Inquisitions / Breaking Into Wall Street | length: 17:51 | cluster: funds | workflow: Private equity fund performance analysis for LPs (TVPI/DPI/IRR, fund evaluation, pacing)

[00:00] Welcome to another tutorial video. We're going to go back to one of my favorite topics today, which is private equity fund performance, and how you can judge it with a series of different metrics such as TVPI, total value to paid in capital, the multiple of invested capital, the distributions to paid in capital or DPI, and then variations of IRR such as the gross versus the net numbers. In this tutorial, we are going to go through an Excel file here, a simplified view of what a private equity fund and its portfolio companies might actually look like. I'm going to start by taking you through some of the concepts and
[00:32] then in the second part, we'll go into it in a little bit more detail, and I'll show you some of the formulas and calculations. Now, obviously, you can find the basic definitions of all these terms online, but I want to go a step beyond that here and actually show you what it looks like in Excel and also how you might interpret these numbers. People like to debate the best metric for judging private equity performance, but that sort of misses the point. The real questions you have to ask are what stage is the fund at in its life cycle, what strategies is it using, and then what assumptions back up the metrics that
[01:04] you're calculating for the fund. If you don't have this information, none of these metrics mean anything because you have no idea how reliable they are or where they're coming from or what they actually mean relative to the fund's life cycle. So, you need all this information first before you can say much. If you want the files and resources here, including the Excel file, you can go to this URL on screen on our financial sponsors page, private equity fund performance metrics. I'll pin this as the first comment below the video, so you can click it right there and get all the files. This is a summary from our full private equity funds of
[01:36] funds and secondaries course, and you can get detailed case studies in that course. So I've prepared this table on some of the key performance metrics for private equity funds from gross value to net value to net asset value to the gross MOIC and gross IRR to TVPI net IRR DPI and RVPI. And I have all the definitions here on screen. Let's start with gross IRR and gross MOIC because I think these are probably the most straightforward metrics. With these, what you're essentially looking at is how much the private equity fund has invested in portfolio
[02:09] companies total over its life cycle so far. And then you're comparing that to the unrealized values of the portfolio companies that it has not yet sold plus the realized values of any portfolio companies that it has sold. And the gross multiple of invested capital just takes the realizations plus the unrealized values and divides by all the invested capital so far. And in this case, they get to about 1.9x. just under double their money is what everything is worth so far. And then the gross irra, we just apply the standard IR function. This gives us a rough sense of what the
[02:41] annualized rate of return is based on all these investments and then what the portfolio companies are worth in the final year including the one that we've sold and the ones that we have not sold. The most important thing with these metrics is that they do include both realized and unrealized portfolio companies. So they differ from a metric like DPI that focuses on just the realized portfolio companies. Now what makes private equity fund analysis more complicated than this is the fees. They tend to be extremely high in private equity and they cause a lot of
[03:13] complications. There are the management fees that are typically a small percentage of the fund size, usually about 2% or the committed capital in the investment period. And then these scale down to maybe 1 to 1.5% and they're based on the remaining cost basis of the portfolio companies after the investment period. There's also carry or carried interest, which is normally 20% of the investment profits roughly speaking and it's paid to the professionals at the private equity firm, but it is subject to minimum return requirements as well. If you look at the file here, you can see that we've calculated the management
[03:45] fees based on 2% of the committed capital in the investment period. And then after that, we have about 4.7 billion left in portfolio companies. And so we switch to 1.5% times that to get to the management fee in year six. For the carried interest, it's a little bit more complicated than the definition I laid out because you also have to factor in the management fees. But if you do that and then you multiply by the 20% carried interest, you can get an idea of what it is for the one portfolio company that has been sold and then all the other portfolio companies that have not
[04:17] yet been sold. We can take that gross value from the unrealized plus realized companies, deduct the carried interest and then get to the net value after that. Now once we have those fees, we can estimate some of the net metrics. There's the TVPI or the net value divided by the called capital. This essentially means that we subtract the carried interest acred and paid out in the numerator and then in the denominator we count not just the amounts that have been invested into portfolio companies but also the management fees. So if you look at the calculation right here TVPI
[04:52] we are adding up the net value which I just showed you on screen. So everything that has been sold, all the unsold companies values, we deduct the realized carried interest and the acred carried interest and then we divide by the total called capital. And if you look at what the called capital represents right here, it's essentially whatever we have invested in [clears throat] the portfolio companies and then also the management fees. There's the net IRRa which is like the gross IRRa except it factors in fees and carried interest. You always use the net cash flows here. So you're always taking
[05:25] the net value and then you're netting it against the called capital. You can see how the net cash flows here are always less than the gross cash flows and therefore the net IRRa should always be less than the gross irra at least if the fund has been around for any length of time. Beyond that there is the DPI which equals the previous realizations. So the portfolio companies the fund has sold so far minus the distributed carry divided by the called capital. This one is sort of like a cash in versus cash out metric as of the fund's current deed. So if we go and look at the calculation here, we
[05:58] are essentially taking everything that has been sold. So the one portfolio company in this case for 1.4 billion, we are deducting the 187.5 million of carried interest that we paid out on that. And then we're dividing by the called capital. So everything we've invested in portfolio companies and also all the management fees that our fund has charged that our fund has called from our limited partners. In this case it's 2x which is on the low side but it's also only year 6 of year 10. So it's not that unusual. What do all these metrics mean? Well the first thing I
[06:30] would point out is that it's really hard to say much of anything because when you look at the unrealized values here we have no idea what kind of assumptions are going into these. We don't know what multiples they're being valued at, what the growth rates look like, what the financials look like. So, it's hard to say much of anything there. The low DPI of 2x is not necessarily concerning because this is year six of a 10-year fund. And so, we'd expect it to be relatively low in the beginning and then to really start ramping up in the last few years. Now, if we get to year 10 and the DPI is still only 2x, that is a giant red flag. But in year six, we'd
[07:04] say that this is a little bit concerning, but not necessarily a red flag. The gross to net gap is normal. There's about a 6 or 7% difference between gross and net IRRa because of the fees. And overall, we'd say the fund has been solid, but not spectacular. The gross IRRa is about what private equity firms usually target, just over 20%. The net irr is above the historical average annualized return for the S&amp;P 500, depending on the period that you look at, but it's not beating it necessarily by a huge margin. Again, depending on the period you look at, the assumptions
[07:35] you use, and things like that, but that's what we'd say overall. So, now that we've been through that introduction, I want to go through each of these points in a little bit more detail. We'll start with the fee calculations and formulas. Then, we'll talk about the net metrics, and I'll show you how to calculate each one of these on screen. And then, we'll go through some points that make this more complicated, including portfolio company valuations, waterfall schedules, and fund recycling. So, as I mentioned, the management fees seem very simple on the surface. 2% 1.5% 1% of pretty easily trackable numbers. But the hard part is
[08:07] that you often have to allocate these to specific companies to calculate the carried interest for that one company. One method is to take a weighted average of each company's contribution to the total cost basis over the funds life so far. So what that means in Excel is that if we go back, I've pulled up a version here where I've deleted this is that we can go in and we can take the total management fees right here and we can just split them up and say that some of these correspond to Cyber Sentinel AI and then the rest correspond to all the unsold portfolio companies. So we can just do a summation of the cost basis
[08:40] for Cyber Sentinel AI and then divide by the total cost basis for all the other companies. This gives us sort of a timew weighted average of this one company's contribution over time. It's about 62 or 63 million. And then the management fees for all the other companies equal the total minus whatever we've allocated to this one company that we've sold. So it's about 578 million right here. The carried interest is normally based on 20% of the realizations plus the unrealized value minus the invested capital minus the allocated management fees. It is subject to the hurdle rate
[09:13] check. usually 80% but we're ignoring that here. Normally we have to calculate it separately for realized companies but we can group the unrealized companies together. This depends a little bit on the fund structure though. We're simplifying here though and not really paying too much attention to that. Now one other small fix or enhancement I could make here is to put a min zero around this. The reason we do that is because for example if we sell this company at a loss for 300 million let's say we don't want the carried interest here to be positive. So one easy way to fix this is to go in and to say min zero around this whole thing. And that will ensure that this is going to only be a negative number. It can't turn into a positive
[10:50] number even if we sell Cyber Sentinel AI at a loss. I'm going to change this back to 1.4 billion for now. Now for the accured carried interest, it is quite similar. So we're going to go and get our gross values right here. I'll just sum up all of these and then we are going to subtract the called capital because this represents everything that we've invested into these companies and all the management fees. And remember the bulk of the management fees are allocated to these unrealized portfolio companies. Let's put parentheses around this
[11:25] and let's multiply by the carried interest and then let's subtract the realized carried interest right here because we are looking at this based on the total gross value. But remember that some of these this carried interest has already been paid out. So we need to subtract this and we get to that. And I need to flip the sign here. So I'll do that right now. And once again, I could put a min zero around this whole thing just to make sure that if we are doing really really poorly, we're recording a loss. This can never turn into a
[11:58] positive number. And we have that. And now we can add this up and get to our net value numbers down here at the bottom. So that's a little bit more about the fee calculations and formulas. Now let's look at the net metrics and go through some of the calculations for these. So normally you want to have a setup where you have the invested capital, the called capital, the unrealized values, the realized values and the carried interest at the bottom as we currently have. Then you can calculate the gross and net cash flows. The gross cash flows are just the gross values minus the invested capital. Net cash flows are net values minus the called capital. So let's go in and do
[12:31] this. We'll take the gross cash flows first. I'll just get the invested capital right up here and then the gross value right there. And then for the net cash flows, we'll get the called capital and we'll net it against the total net value right there. We can also calculate the net asset value. We don't really need it for anything at this point, but it is useful to look at this metric. It's the unrealized values of the remaining portfolio companies that have not yet been sold. And then we deduct the acred carried interest rate there. So with that set up, we now have everything we need to calculate the TVPI, the DPI, and everything else down here. So let's go
[13:04] through these calculations. For the gross multiple of invested capital, we're just going to take all the gross values up here and then we're going to divide it by the sum of the invested capital right there. For the gross internal rate of return, we just apply the IRRa function to the gross cash flows. And for the net IRR, we apply it to the net cash flows right here. For the TVPI, the total value to paid in capital, this is like the grossest multiple invested capital, but it's calculated on a net basis after the fees. So we take the net value and then we go up and divide by the called capital right here because this reflects
[13:35] the management fees as well as the investments into portfolio companies and then for the distributions to paid in capital. So this one focuses on just the realizations and the distributed carried interest. So let's go and put a negative in front and then I'll take the sum of all of our realizations right here. We will then deduct the realized carried interest that we've paid out associated with those and then we'll divide by the called capital right up here and we have that and then the RVPI is just the TVPI minus the DPI
[14:08] and this gives us a measure of how much value is remaining in this PE fund to be realized in the future or to potentially be realized in the future if we believe in this fund's valuations. So that's a little bit more about the calculations for these metrics. Now what makes this analysis more complicated? because so far it might seem fairly simple. First off, one big issue is that you often have to challenge the private equity fund's valuation assumptions. So I have up here an example from a secondaries case study in our course, but essentially here the private equity fund was valuing this company at a pretty
[14:42] high revenue multiple of around 8 to 9x. Now, this is a high growth software SAS company, but we felt it was too high looking at the public comps. And so, we reduced the multiple down to more like the 7 to 8x range over the future. And this is a pretty mild adjustment, but this is the type of thing you might have to do. And so, the unrealized values might end up being quite different. Hurdle rates, preferred returns, and catch-up returns can also complicate things quite a bit. I have up here an example from our course where we start by returning capital to limited partners. Then we give them a preferred return of 8% per year of their capital.
[15:18] If there's enough left after that, we catch the GPS up, so the professionals of the private equity firm, and they get returns up to the 8%. And then once everyone is caught up, then we do a profit split of 80/20 and we distribute the carried interest like that. Now, this is not super complicated, but it does take time. And if you have to set it up for each portfolio company, it's just something else to check in your model. And then a third complexity is that you can see more complex fund terms and policies such as fund recycling. You can have clawbacks if a fund ends up underperforming after the carried
[15:49] interest has already been paid out. There can be penalty fees as well. with fund recycling. Just to show you a simple example, if we have a fund that has invested 86 million out of 100 million of cold capital, but they get an early distribution for 20 million, they could potentially take this and then reinvest it into a portfolio company so that they end up investing 106 million rather than 86 million of capital. And so that would change the numbers and some of these calculations as well. So this is an example of what can make the analysis more complicated. You could
[16:21] also make the formulas and the schedules here a lot more robust and flexible and that also adds the complexity. So that's about it. Let's do a quick recap and summary with the fee calculations and formulas. The main thing here is that with management fees, the basic idea is simple, but you often have to allocate them to specific companies. So you have to take some type of time weighted average as we did. With carried interest, if you're not factoring in the hurdle rate, it's not that complicated. It's essentially 20% of the investment profits. You do have to factor in the allocated management fees and you do have to make sure that they always have the correct sign, but the hurdle rate is
[16:55] what really makes them complicated. With the net metrics, we went through the TVPI, DPI, and net IRRa calculations. The TVPI is essentially like the multiple of invested capital after the carried interest and management fees. The DPI focuses on the cash in and cash out. So everything that they have invested, everything that they've charged in terms of management fees and then you compare that to the realizations minus the distributed carried interest on those realizations and then the net IRRa is the annualized return after the management fees and carried interest. What makes this more complicated are challenging the PE funds
[17:28] valuation assumptions, setting up waterfall schedules, and also fund recycling. So that's about it for this lesson. Hopefully now you know a little bit more about how to measure PE fund performance and some of the subtleties that come up with formulas when you try to set up the schedule in Excel.

[C] Fund Balance Analysis
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qoQGoaSSck
channel: Lake Superior State University | length: 12:25 | cluster: public | workflow: Government fund accounting: GASB 34 conversion, fund balance, year-end close, budget-to-actual
====================================================================================================
[00:02] hi I'm Rebecca clawen the finance specialist for the charter school office at Lake Superior State University I'm going to be doing a PowerPoint presentation on fund balance as part of a series of uh short videos that we'll be producing for our Academy boards this PowerPoint presentation will be available on our website if you would like to print it or follow along our website where you can find that is www. lssu.edu Charter fund balance in its most simple
[00:46] definition is the difference between assets and liabilities on the balance sheet it is comprised of any existing fund balance at the beginning of the reporting period coupled with the net change in the income statement for that reporting period essentially it's what's left over after the fund's assets have been used to satisfy the fund's liabilities sometimes it's difficult to give a definitive answer as to how fund balance should be interpreted because different users of the financial statements have different needs for example a financial institution that's
[01:20] considering lending funds to an academy will interpret fund balance differently than say a parent at a school board meeting given these differences and inter interpretation there are some fundamentals to consider when trying to analyze fund balance one such fundamental is that fund balance is only reported in the governmental funds not for any proprietary funds or for the Academy as a whole the best way to Envision fund balance is in terms of the fund it is associated with for example a special Revenue fund exists for a
[01:55] specific Revenue source and the uses of those resources so the remainder after the liabilities have been satisfied would be a fund bounds with certain limitations imposed on it since June 15th of 2011 the governmental Accounting Standards Board has required implementation of gby pronouncement number 54 this pronouncement reclassified fund balance designations from reserved and unreserved into five new categories these new categories are
[02:28] presented on the Bal balance sheet in a hierarchy from most to least restricted we'll have more on the fund types of classifications later on in the presentation this is an example of an annual audit of a combined statement of Revenue expenditures and changes in fund bounds it's also known as an income statement it shows all the revenues and expenditures for each governmental fund that the academy operates
[03:00] as I stated earlier essentially fund balance is the residual amount left after the funds assets have been used to satisfy the fund's liabilities which is why the change from this statement is added to the beginning fund balance for the reporting period in the example the circled area represents this change the beginning fund balance for the period is shown in the circled area which is combined with the beginning fund balance
[03:32] that combined figure is the ending fund balance for the reporting period this ending fund balance is carried over to the balance sheet for the reporting period this is an example of an annual audit of the combined governmental balance sheet it shows all the assets liabilities and fund balance for each governmental fund that the academy operates earlier I mentioned that fund balance is the difference between assets and
[04:05] liabilities which is represented by the equation assets equals liabilities and fund balance the total fund balance for each fund presented must match the ending fund balance from the statement of revenues expenditures and changes in fund balance which is the statement that was on the slide before this you can see how the fund balance in the circled area matches that some of the new categories of fund balance introduced in gasby number 54 are shown in this
[04:38] example the next few slides we'll discuss each of the new designations of fund balance prior to June 15th 2011 fund balance was designated into two types reserved and unreserved with reserved having two categories designated and and undesignated after June 15th 2011 gby pronouncement number 54 requires designations into five categories into just
[05:11] two these new designations are presented in descending order from the most restricted to the least restricted the first three are nonspendable restricted and committed they are most similar to the old classification of reserved the last two are assigned and unassigned they are most similar to the previous classification of unreserved designated and unreserved undesignated these are the least
[05:43] restricted types of fund balance nonspendable is the category of fund balance that is the most restricted because these amounts are not in spendable form which means that they are not expected to be converted into Cash usually represented by something like inventory or prepaid items nonspendable is also not in spendable form because they are legally required to remain intact for example a corpus or the principle of a Permanent
[06:18] Fund restricted fund balance is segregated based on a specific purpose by either an external party or imposed by law the definition of restricted fund balance is the same as the definition used in gby number 34 for restricted net assets net assets are the Academy as a whole an example would be a principal payment in a Debt Service fund for a bond indenture committed fund balance are
[06:52] amounts designated for a specific purpose based on the action of the academy itself in other words formal action taken by the school board such as a resolution a resolution to designate resources as committed fund balance must occur prior to the end of the fiscal year however if the dollar amount hasn't been decided upon that can be known later the same formal action is required to change the amount or to remove the designation assign fund balance for all
[07:30] governmental funds except the general fund a sign fund balance is any residual amount not classified as nonspendable restricted or committed a sign fund balance for any fund except the general fund must be positive for the general fund a signed fund balance is the amount that the academy itself or an official of the academy with the authority to assign amounts has intended for a specific purpose this intent is not a commitment because it is not required to have a
[08:04] formal resolution any fund with assigned fund balance cannot result in a deficit unassigned fund balance they must remain positive unassigned fund balance this is the least restricted fund balance designation within the general fund unassigned is a catch off for any amounts that are not already segregated such as nonspendable restricted committed or assigned the general fund should be the
[08:37] only fund with a positive unassigned fund balance any other fund that reports an unassigned fund balance would report it as a deficit when it comes to deciding on the classification between the five different types of fund balance it's usually safe to assume that the classification should represent the nature of the designation for example in a Debt Service fund the payment of principal on an outstanding Bond would need to be segregated based on the fact
[09:10] that those resources would be used to satisfy the payment so a restricted fund balance would be appropriate for that transaction not all Academy governmental funds will have every type of fund balance designation each Academy should Rev their policies regarding which types of funds are used first if no policy has been adopted then the default usage would begin with committed then assigned then
[09:41] unassigned one of the most common questions regarding fund balance that I get is how much should we have this is a great question but there are so many different answers the short answer is to make sure that in the event that there was a loss of Revenue there would be enough to meet the liabilities of the academy until another funding source can be obtained another really good resource I found is from the Michigan school business officials they recommend that schools maintain a fund balance of 15% of the general fund
[10:14] expenditures also try to remember that it takes time to build up a fund balance a new school may not have such a large fund balance but over time could accumulated to a comfortable amount a school can also consult with their external Auditors to obtain a recommendation and perhaps adopt a policy regarding a minimum fund balance certain disclosures are required in the notes of the audited financial statements for each Academy such policies regarding
[10:46] expenditures a minimum fund balance requirement or a description of the authority required to designate fund balance your external auditor will be able to assist with the required note closures this is an example of what the different types of fund balances in the governmental funds may look like note the descending order from the most to the least restricted beginning with nonspendable and ending with unassigned again not all governmental
[11:18] funds will have all five types of fund balances resources there are so many great available resources including the governmental Accounting Standards Board which is the very first website posted up here the gasby dorg another favorite resource that I like to use is the Michigan public school accounting manual that can be found electronically on the state of Michigan's Department of Education website I use that very frequently as a
[11:52] resource your external Auditors I can't recommend them enough as a great source of knowledge and experience also myself if you have any questions or you need clarification on any kind of subject I would be more than happy to assist you please contact me at my direct number which is 906 635 2279 or feel free to email me my email is posted on this page it's R clawen lssu.edu thank you for your participation and have a great day

[00:00] Airports sell bonds with an official statement. An official statement can run to several hundred pages. Tampa's 2024 preliminary official statement ran to 444, counting its appendices. What should an investor read first? This is Airport Debt and Credit, Part 6: Reading an Official Statement. This series is produced by DWU Consulting, with AI-assisted narration. Please send us your comments by email: dwu@dwuconsulting.com An airport runs on three rule books at once.
[00:33] The first is accounting: generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), set by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board. The second is rates and charges: the airline agreement or rate resolution that sets what airlines pay. The third is the bond trust: the bond documents, which set what bondholders are promised. Each rule book defines the same words its own way. Revenues, expenses, debt service and coverage can mean different things in each. In an official statement, a capitalized word like Revenues is a defined term. Find its definition in that document.
[01:09] An illustrative example, not any real airport. Operating revenues are $100 million. Operating expenses before depreciation are $60 million. Depreciation is $30 million. Under accounting rules, operating income is $10 million, because depreciation counts as an expense. A typical bond document leaves depreciation out. If its defined Revenues and Operating Expenses match these figures, net revenues are $40 million. Same airport, same year: $10 million under accounting
[01:43] rules, or $40 million under the bond document. Two documents do most of the work: the annual comprehensive financial report, and the official statement. The annual report tells what happened. It is audited, prepared under accounting rules, and published some months after the fiscal year ends. It belongs to the accounting rule book. The official statement is written when the airport sells bonds. It describes the pledge, the rate covenant, the flow of funds and a summary of the airline agreement. It belongs to the bond trust rule book.
[02:16] It also looks forward. Many include a report by an airport consultant, with forecasts of traffic, revenue and coverage. So the annual report reports the past. The official statement sets out the legal terms and projects the future. Read together, they answer a simple question. Did the airport do what its last official statement said it would? In the annual report, start with the auditor's opinion. Look for a modified opinion, or a paragraph that flags going concern or a restatement. Next, management's discussion and analysis.
[02:50] Check that its story matches the numbers. Then the statement of revenues, expenses and changes in net position: airline revenue, non-airline revenue, and operating expenses. Airline payments there are the output of a rate formula, so new debt service in the rate base raises them. Parking and concession revenue move with traffic and the market. Then the notes: the debt schedule, pensions and other retiree benefits, leases, and contingent liabilities. Last, the statistical section: up to ten years of traffic, revenue,
[03:23] debt and coverage. It is not audited. Coverage in that section is measured after the year closes. It may follow the bond documents or another basis, so check the basis stated with the table. At a pure residual airport, coverage is built into the rate formula, so it is set in advance rather than earned. A change from one year to the next there is often accounting mechanics, not stress. At a hybrid residual airport, coverage is only partly built in. Now the official statement. Where should an investor start?
[03:55] Start with the rate covenant, because it tells you which definitions matter. Then read the defined terms it uses. A definition that the covenant, the flow of funds and the additional bonds test do not use can wait. In Tampa's 2024 preliminary official statement, the rate covenant is on printed page 13. It requires Revenues enough to make the required deposits to the operating and reserve funds, plus 125 percent of the Bond Service Requirement. Bond Service Requirement is a defined term. Its definition is in Appendix C, the trust agreement.
[04:30] Then read the pledge and the flow of funds: which revenues secure the bonds, and who is paid first. The front text, and the official statement's summary of the bond documents, are first-hand legal disclosure. The newest official statement outranks an older indenture, because it reflects later amendments. The report of the airport consultant is different. It is the consultant's interpretation and forecast: useful, but second-hand. Part 7 of this series covers it. The official statement also summarizes the airline agreement. That summary is the bondholders' view,
[05:04] and it may be out of date. For how rates are calculated today, go to the current agreement or the rate resolution. Tampa's airline rates come from a resolution, and that preliminary official statement attaches the resolution itself as Appendix E. The official statement also describes the additional bonds test, a bond-document test for issuing more bonds on the same pledge. Part 3 of this series covered it. Three traps catch careful readers. First, the year. An official statement's date is not the fiscal year of its data.
[05:38] Tampa's preliminary official statement, dated August 2024, carries audited statements through the fiscal year ended September 30, 2023. Read the fiscal year printed on each table. Second, coverage is not one number. Coverage under the bond documents and coverage in airline rate setting can differ, and analysts compute their own versions too. Some reported coverage counts transfers from reserves, sometimes the whole balance of certain unrestricted funds. Some counts net revenues alone. Read the basis stated with the table before you compare
[06:13] airports. Third, days cash on hand. Bond documents do not define it, so two figures are not comparable until you know each one's basis. So every days cash on hand figure needs its basis stated: which cash counts, and which expenses it is measured against. To recap. Three rule books, accounting, rates and charges, and the bond trust, define the same words differently. Check which one you are reading. The annual report tells what happened, under accounting rules. The official statement sets out the bond terms and projects the future.

The consultant's report is second-hand, and the airline agreement holds the rate formula. Check the fiscal year of every table, and the basis of every coverage or cash figure. [01:08] places where an organization's financial data must be presented according to Gap or generally accepted accounting principles a common set of accounting rules to keep financial reporting consistent from one organization to the next Gap standards for a nonprofit audit require four financial statements and in this order first we have the statement of financial position this is also known in the for-profit or corporate sector as
[01:42] the balance sheet and we typically refer to it even in the nonprofit sector as the balance sheet next we have the statement of activities which is known in the corporate sector as the income statement or the profit and loss the PNF next we have the statement of functional expenses this is not known as anything in the corporate sector because there is no equivalent of the statement of functional expenses in a for-profit

[02:47] financial statements and we'll talk a little bit about what is included in those notes so now what I'm going to do is walk through each of these four financial statements beginning with the statement of financial position so the statement of financial position or the balance sheet consists of three components we have assets liabilities and net assets so our assets are simply what we own as an organization including cash
[03:23] receivables Investments property equipment anything that we own as an organization is an asset on our balance sheet liabilities are what we owe to parties outside the organization so this is bills due a line of credit any debt mortgages anything like that is a liability on the balance sheet and the difference between assets and liabilities are called net assets
[03:59] you might think of net assets as the net worth of an organization in the same way you might consider the net worth if we were looking at our personal or individual finances the difference between our assets and liabilities would be our net worth in the corporate sector this is called Equity or shareholders Equity the difference between assets and liabilities in the nonprofit sector are called net assets as we will see

[09:38] purpose like future capital projects or other potential Investments while the board may have placed requirements on Management in order to access those assets they're still not considered restricted from an accounting perspective since remember only the donor can restrict RCT Revenue therefore board designated net assets can be shown as a subset of net assets without donor restrictions so those are the different

[26:22] flow actually looks back at the previous year and shows where our cash came from and how it was used it's not the same as a cash flow projection which is a forward-looking financial document that projects cash coming in and cash going out over the course of the coming months or weeks the statement of cash flows is a backward-looking statement that covers what happened over the course of the past period the past year in this case if you're applying for a loan or a line
[26:55] of credit the statement of cash flows will get some some scrutiny from your lender but from a day-to-day financial management perspective a forward-looking cash projection is likely a more effective planning tool so here's what a statement of cash flow looks like it reports on cash coming in and cash going out from your operations so there is a section of cash flows from operating activities from Investments and investing activities including in investments in fixed assets

[C] Decoding IRS Form 990-PF Part 1: Reading Foundation Filings
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7k8TOimybvA
channel: Angel Reyes DrPH (c), MCHES, PMP, ACP | length: 19:30 | cluster: public | workflow: Nonprofit financial analysis from Form 990 / audited statements (grant due diligence, 990-PF)
