[00:00] Welcome to lesson 2.5 of the grant architect course. In this lesson and the next, we will develop skills for analyzing IRS form 9990, specifically form 990 PF filed by private foundations. Tax returns are primary sources that reveal what foundations actually do versus what they say they do. While database profiles and website descriptions provide useful summaries, 990s provide ground truth about foundation finances, governance, and giving patterns. In this first part, we
[00:33] will focus on accessing public tax records through platforms like Guidear, Candid, and ProPublica, and understanding basic foundation information, including assets, payout rates, and board composition. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to locate and access Foundation 990s and extract key organizational information from them. Form 990 PF is the specific tax form that private foundations must file, distinct from the form 990 filed by public charities. Understanding the PF designation helps
[01:07] you search for the right documents. Private foundations, whether independent, family, or corporate foundations, file form 990 PF. Public charities, including community foundations, file Form 990. The forms differ significantly, so knowing which type you need matters for research. Annual filing is required. Foundations must file their 990 PF within approximately 4 and a half months after their fiscal year ends. This annual cadence means new information becomes available. predictably, though with some
[01:40] lag. Public document status is key for research. While individual tax returns are private, nonprofit and foundation tax returns are public documents. Congress mandated this transparency to ensure public accountability for taxexempt organizations. This transparency enables the prospect research we are learning. Comprehensive data in 990 PFS includes financial information such as assets, income, and expenses, governance information such as
[02:12] board members and key employees, and grant-making information such as grants paid during the year. Learning to extract this information is essential for foundation research. Several platforms provide access to Foundation 990s, each with different strengths. ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer is free and provides comprehensive access to 990 data. You can search by organization name, view financial summaries, and download actual 990 PDF files. ProPublica is an excellent starting
[02:45] point for 990 research, especially for those without database subscriptions. Guidear, now part of Candid, provides searchable profiles with linked 990s. Basic Access is free, showing summary information. Premium access provides additional features. The integration of 990 data with organizational profiles makes Guidear valuable for research. The IRS taxexempt organization search is the direct source from the IRS. While less userfriendly than commercial platforms,
[03:17] it provides authoritative access to filed returns. If you cannot find a 990 elsewhere, check the IRS database directly. Some foundation websites post their own 990s as part of transparency commitments. Before searching external databases, check whether the foundation you are researching makes its returns available directly. This can provide the most current information. The 990 PF contains multiple parts, each providing different types of information. Learning to navigate efficiently helps you find
[03:50] what you need. Part one provides a summary of financial activities, including revenue, expenses, and dispersements for charitable purposes. This high-level overview shows the foundation's overall financial activity during the year. Part two presents the balance sheet showing assets, liabilities, and net assets. This section reveals the foundation's financial capacity. Asset size indicates the scale of resources available for grant making, helping you assess whether your request size is realistic. Part seven a lists officers, directors,
[04:24] trustees, and key employees along with their compensation. This section reveals who governs the foundation and makes decisions. Knowing board composition can inform relationship building strategies. Part 15th lists grants and contributions paid during the year. This is often the most valuable section for prospect research, showing exactly what the foundation funded. We will explore part 15 in depth in the next lesson. Other parts provide additional information about investments, financial activities, and compliance. For prospect research,
[04:59] parts 1, 2, 7, A, and X are typically most relevant. Understanding foundation assets helps you assess giving capacity and appropriate request sizes. Total assets represent the foundation's total financial resources, primarily investments. Part two of the 990 PF shows total assets at year end. This figure provides context for understanding the foundation scale and capacity. Fair market value shows the current value of investments and
[05:31] property rather than original purchase prices. For investments like stocks, fair market value fluctuates with markets. The 990 PF reports both book value and fair market value for key asset categories. Asset size categories help classify foundations. A foundation with 10 million in assets is quite different from one with 10 billion. Understanding where a foundation falls in the size spectrum helps you calibrate expectations for grant sizes and competition levels. Payout implications connect assets to giving capacity.
[06:04] Private foundations must generally pay out approximately 5% of their investment assets annually for charitable purposes. This means you can roughly estimate annual giving capacity from asset size. A foundation with 100 million in assets might give approximately 5 million annually. Analyzing financial trends requires reviewing multiple years of 990s rather than just the most recent. Multi-year review provides context that single-year data cannot. A foundation's assets and giving in any single year may be
[06:38] unusual. Reviewing 3 to 5 years of 990s reveals typical patterns and trends. Most platforms providing 990 access retain multiple years of filings. Asset trajectory shows whether the foundation is growing or shrinking. Are assets increasing over time as investment returns exceed payouts. Are they decreasing as the foundation spends down? Growth suggests sustained giving capacity. Spending down suggests the foundation may eventually close. Giving patterns reveal whether grant making is
[07:11] increasing, decreasing, or stable. Some foundations increase giving over time as assets grow. Others maintain consistent giving. Some reduce giving due to financial challenges. Understanding trends helps you assess future giving likelihood. Stability assessment examines how consistent foundation activity is. Large year-to-year fluctuations might indicate instability or unusual circumstances. Consistent patterns suggest predictability. Stable foundations may be more reliable
[07:45] long-term funding prospects. Board and leadership information in part 7A reveals who governs the foundation and potentially makes grant-making decisions. Part 7A location is where you find officers, directors, trustees, and foundation managers. The form lists names, titles, hours worked, and compensation. This section provides the official record of foundation governance. Compensation data shows whether positions are paid or volunteer. Many family foundation board members serve without compensation. Larger
[08:18] foundations may have paid staff and compensated board members. Compensation patterns suggest the foundation's professionalization level. Board composition reveals who governs and influences decisions. Are board members all from one family? Are there independent members? Are there subject matter experts? Board composition affects how decisions are made and what perspectives influence grant making. Connection opportunities emerge from knowing who is involved with foundations. Do you know anyone on the board? Do your board members know them?
[08:52] Can you find connection pathways through mutual contacts? Board information can inform relationship building strategies. Understanding payout requirements helps you interpret foundation behavior and assess capacity. The 5% rule requires private foundations to distribute approximately 5% of their non-charitable use investment assets annually for charitable purposes. This requirement ensures foundations actually use their assets for public benefit rather than simply accumulating wealth. Qualifying distributions count toward the
[09:25] requirement. These include grants to other organizations, direct charitable activities, and certain administrative expenses related to charitable programs. Not all foundation spending counts. There are specific rules about what qualifies. Payout calculation determines the minimum distribution amount. The calculation is based on average fair market value of investment assets, not total assets. Foundations may distribute more than the minimum, but must meet at least this threshold. Strategic implications follow from understanding
[09:58] these constraints. Foundations near their minimum payout may have limited flexibility for new grants. Foundations paying well above minimums have more capacity. Understanding payout context helps you assess whether a foundation can realistically add new grantees or is already stretched to meet requirements. Reading financial health indicators helps you assess foundation stability and capacity. Investment income shows returns on foundation investments. Foundations typically invest their
[10:30] assets and use investment returns to fund operations and grant making. Strong investment returns support sustained giving. Poor returns may constrain giving capacity. Administrative expenses reveal operating costs relative to grant making. Some administrative expenses are normal and necessary. Very high ratios of administrative expenses to grant making might suggest inefficiency or concern. Industry norms provide benchmarks for reasonable expense ratios. Excise taxes and penalties indicate compliance issues if present.
[11:02] Private foundations pay a small excise tax on investment income which is normal. Additional taxes or penalties might indicate compliance problems. Review tax payment sections for anything unusual. The overall picture emerges from considering these indicators together. Is the foundation financially healthy with strong assets, good returns, reasonable expenses, and clean compliance? Or are there warning signs suggesting instability? Financial health affects likelihood of sustained grant
[11:35] making. Family foundations have distinct characteristics identifiable through 990 analysis. Board composition in family foundations typically includes family members in governance roles. If the board consists entirely of people with the same last name, it is likely a family foundation. Family governance often means personal relationships influence grant-making decisions. Foundation names often include the family name. The Smith Family Foundation or John and Mary Smith Foundation clearly indicate family origin. Even
[12:08] when foundations have non-family names, board composition usually reveals family involvement. Location often reflects where the founding family lives or lived. Family foundations frequently focus giving on communities important to the family. A foundation based in Minneapolis with primarily Minneapolis area giving likely reflects family connections to that community. Giving patterns in family foundations may reflect family interests and personal connections rather than systematic strategic philanthropy. A family foundation might fund their alma
[12:41] modders, their religious institutions, and causes reflecting personal passions. Understanding family foundation dynamics helps you assess fit and relationship building approaches. Corporate foundations have distinct characteristics identifiable through 990 analysis. Corporate connection is usually evident through name and address. The Acme Corporation Foundation located at Acme headquarters clearly indicates corporate origin. Foundation names typically include or reference the
[13:14] parent company name. Funding source appears in the 990s revenue section. Corporate foundations typically receive contributions from their parent corporations rather than relying solely on investment returns. Annual contributions from the corporation show the ongoing corporate funding relationship. Board composition often includes company executives. Corporate foundation boards frequently include senior executives from the parent company. This composition links foundation priorities to corporate
[13:46] interests and decision-making. Giving alignment with corporate interests is common. Corporate foundations often fund in communities where the company operates, support causes related to the company's industry, or focus on issues affecting the company's workforce or customers. Recognizing corporate foundation patterns helps you identify alignment opportunities related to the parent company. Identifying foundation type through 990 analysis helps you tailor your approach. Pass through versus endowed foundations differ in how
[14:18] they fund grant making. Pass through foundations receive and distribute contributions in the same year, often from corporations or living donors. Endowed foundations have permanent investments generating returns that fund grant making. The revenue and asset sections of the 990 reveal which type you are dealing with. Operating versus grant-making foundations differ in primary activity. Operating foundations primarily run their own charitable programs rather than making grants to others. Grant-making foundations
[14:50] primarily distribute funds to other organizations. Part nine and part 15th help distinguish these types. Operating foundations may be poor prospects for grants. Active versus minimal operation affects capacity. Some foundations actively seek grantees, employ staff, and engage strategically. Others minimally operate, making grants to satisfy legal requirements without active engagement. Grant-making activity levels, staffing, and administrative expenses indicate engagement level.
[15:23] Strategic implications vary by foundation type. Endowed grant-making foundations with active engagement are typically the strongest prospects for competitive grants. Other types may require different approaches or may not be strong prospects. Understanding common mistakes helps you use 990s more effectively. Single-year analysis misses important trends. Any single year might be unusual. Multi-year analysis reveals patterns that single years obscure. Always try to review several years of 990s for any foundation
[15:58] you are seriously researching. Ignoring context misses important explanations for what you observe. A foundation's assets might drop due to market declines, not spending down. Giving might spike due to a one-time disaster response grant. Consider broader economic and organizational context when interpreting data. Misreading data produces incorrect conclusions. 990 PF is complex with many line items and calculations. It is easy to misinterpret what a particular line means or to confuse similar sounding items. Take
[16:31] time to understand what you are reading and consult IRS instructions if uncertain. Over reliance on 990s ignores other valuable information sources. 990s provide important data but not the complete picture. Foundation websites, annual reports, direct contact, and peer intelligence all contribute to comprehensive research. Use 990s as one source among several, not the only source. Building 990 research skills requires practice and
[17:05] systematic development. Practice regularly to build proficiency. Like any skill, 990 analysis improves with practice. Review 990s for foundations you are researching, even when you do not urgently need the information. Regular practice builds familiarity with form structure and common patterns. Using multiple foundations for comparison helps you understand ranges and norms. How do large foundations differ from small ones? How do family foundations differ from corporate foundations? Comparing across types and
[17:38] sizes builds contextual understanding. Creating templates develops standard extraction frameworks for the information you need. What key data points do you want to extract from every 990 you review. A consistent template ensures you capture important information and enables comparison across foundations. Staying current matters because IRS forms and requirements evolve over time. Form changes may affect where information appears or how it is reported. Stay aware of significant changes to maintain
[18:10] accurate analysis. Let us summarize what we have covered in this first part of our 990 exploration. Access methods for obtaining 990s include ProPublica nonprofit explorer for free comprehensive access, Guidear and Candid for integrated profiles, and 990S, the IRS tax exempt organization search as the direct source and foundation websites for self-posted returns. Key sections for initial analysis include part one for financial
[18:42] summary, part two for balance sheet and assets, and part 7A for board and leadership information. These sections reveal foundation capacity and governance. Analysis skills covered include understanding assets and payout implications, analyzing financial trends across multiple years, reading governance information, identifying foundation types, and recognizing family and corporate foundation patterns. In our next lesson, we will dive deep into part 15 of form 9990PF, which lists all grants paid during the
[19:15] year. This section is the richest source of information about what foundations actually fund, and we will learn to analyze it systematically to determine median grant sizes, geographic patterns, and giving priorities.

So, in the first when the reporting timeline arrives, what happens that the first grant deadline reporting deadline is missed. The financial reporting deadline for that matter is
[01:39] missed. Uh so, the narrative is there, but it's kind of uh not agreeing with the financial report that is eventually uh brought out. And uh when you look at everything, the grant is technically in compliance because no hard deadline at that point has been violated. It was just a a a report that gives them the first insight of how implementation is doing. So, you know, at this time, nothing is actually noted as visibly wrong.
[02:12] But, looking at it, what happened between the due diligence and that first missed missed deadline is actually not a mystery. The signals were there in the financials before the grant was made. There were sections of the financial statements that the standard due diligence checklist did not ask anyone to look at. And they were hiding in plain sight, because the framework that was being
[02:44] used to read these documents probably was not designed to bring them to the surface. And that's what I want to talk about today. What grantee financial statements actually contain, because I have been sitting on that side. Where the most useful information lives, and what a grant portfolio's perspective trains you to look for that a standard audit review process does not. So, before we go into the documents
[03:16] themselves, it's worth establishing at this point that we are trying to assess when we read the grantee's financials from a grant portfolio perspective, not from the author's perspective. You know, you know, the question is not simply whether the organization is financially healthy in a general sense. The question is whether this organization has the financial infrastructure to deliver on a specific set of program commitments over the period of this
[03:50] grant, while again simultaneously managing whatever health it's on its balance sheet. Those are different questions. So, an organization can be financially healthy by standard metrics and simultaneously be operating a finance function that will struggle under the specific demands of a complex multi-year award like that like the one we are talking about. But then on the flip side, an organization can have a very thin balance sheet and a finance
[04:23] function that is genuinely excellent, organized, and also well-led. The financial statements contains information that speaks to both of these dimensions if you know what you're actually reading. So, what I'm sharing today comes from two decades of sitting inside nonprofits' finance functions, building and repairing these systems and generating these documents, you know. I have seen the documents look like uh
[04:54] like what I'm talking about, and I have seen when the underlying system is sound. And the difference about those two, where it's sound and where it's not, is usually something very subtle, but they are there. So, let's look at the balance sheet. So, the balance sheet, also called the statement of financial position in our in nonprofit accounting for that matter, is the first document to read
[05:26] when you're evaluating a grantee's financial health. And it's the document that contains the most information about organizations the organization's resilience. Most people read it primarily for the reserve number, but there are four other things it tells you that matter more than the reserve position, especially for the portfolio management decision. So, the first is the composition of the
[06:00] net assets. If you net assets in a not-for-profit organizations, they come in three categories. We have the net assets without donor restrictions. We have the net assets with that with donor restrictions. And in some instances, we have permanently restricted net assets. Let's look at now like things like the endowment endowment funds. So, the total assets with donor restrictions and in your financials tells you almost nothing useful without knowing
[06:36] how those assets are split. For example, if you look at the total asset number on the summary page, you will see that okay, this organization has this total net assets. But this one does not tell you anything substantial without knowing how these net assets are are split. So, an organization, for example, with $5 million in total net assets, 4 million of which are permanently restricted in, for example, an endowment funds and 1 million of which
[07:10] are donor restricted in capital projects. You see this this organization has essentially no unrestricted financial flexibility. On the other hand, an organization with the same $5 million in unrestricted net assets has enormous flexibility. This split, it really matters more than the total figure you see at the at the summary page. The second is the relationship between current assets and current liabilities, what we call the current ratio.
[07:41] Basically, this is the measure that the organization can meet its uh current short-term obligations. So, it's a standard metric that we have to look at, and it's always worth looking at. But, what matters more than this ratio itself is the composition of the current assets. You want to look at cash and short-term investments. Are these because these are are they genuinely liquid, you know? Accounts receivables, for example, from government grants, let's say if the organization is
[08:14] receiving large government grants, or a large foundation, may be sitting there, but it may not be collectible on a timeline that matches the current liabilities that they're being captured against. Again, an organization with a healthy current ratio is built primarily on receivables from like an organization that has uh a healthy current ratio built on receivables from single government contract
[08:46] is at a risk of non-renewal because significantly, you know, this this kind of of grant are very fragile. And so, this kind of of organization is actually also operating on a very fragile ratio. The third is the trend in operating surplus or or deficit. You see, a single year balance sheet shows a snapshot. What you want to see is whether the net assets without donor restrictions have been growing.
[09:17] They've been growing, they've been stable, or they've been eroding over the past 5 years. An organization with a solid reserve position that has been declining by 2 to 5% annually is structurally different. It's in a different situation from one with the same reserve position that has been stable or growing. So, this trend in itself is a signal. When you see at the when you look at the the surplus or deficit from not a single
[09:50] year balance sheet, but a 3-year period balance sheet, you are able to pick a signal because um this snapshot alone is a measurement. Then the fourth and uh this is the one that actually really appears on the standard due diligence checklist is the relationship between deferred revenue and program commitments that it presents. So, we know deferred revenue in it represents uh funds that have been front-loaded, funds
[10:23] that have been received, but the qualifying activities have not been incurred. So, an organization with large deferred revenue balance relative to its operating capacity, you it already signals that it has future program delivery commitments that are already funded and is seated on its balance sheet. So, whether the organization can actually deliver on those commitments is the required in the required trans- time
[10:57] frame of that grant of the funds that have already received within the required conditions is a capacity question that the balance sheet opens, but cannot answer on its own. So, probably something to keep an eye on. And then swiftly moving to the income statement section. So, the statement of activities, which in the nonprofit equivalent of an income statement, tells you about the revenue structure, very important, and the revenue structure is one of the most revealing indicators of
[11:31] organizational stability in a grantee relationship. Why do I say that? The first thing to look at is the revenue concentration. If a single funder represents more than 25 to 30% of total revenue for the organization in a particular year, then the organization definitely has a concentration risk. If a single government contract represents more than 40%, the risk is even more acute in this case because
[12:04] government funding is subject to legislative or sometimes circles that are outside the organization's control. From a portfolio management perspective, funding a highly concentrated grantee creates an interdependency. For example, if their major funder exits or reduces, then the capacity of the organization to deliver on your grant is affected by a decision you had no part in making. The second is the relationship between
[12:38] restricted and unrestricted revenue over time, not just in a particular time period, but over time. So, you find that organizations that are growing their unrestricted revenue base through individual giving, fee for service, or even general operating support from multiple sources are building financial resilience. On the other hand, organizations where revenue is predominantly restricted and predominantly from a smaller number of institutional funders,
[13:13] uh you find that they're finan- they're financially fragile even when the total revenue is substantial. Because the restriction matters uh because restricted funds cannot be used to cover operating infrastructure that makes the delivery of programs possible. An organization that, for example, is 100% restricted is in it in a meaningful sense, it's asking its funders
[13:47] to kind of collectively provide not just program funding, but also the organizational capacity to manage that funding. And very few grant agreements are designed with that understanding explicitly. The third is the pattern of in-kind revenue. So, in-kind revenue is sometimes not given attention, but it's important to check whether it's being used to manage the functional expense ratio. In-kind contributions are legitimate and
[14:19] valuable. It It varies from organization to organization on what they consider as in-kind. The threshold for each organization varies. So, they're also one of the easier mechanisms by which an organization can shift its functional expense ratio without changing any actual cash flows. So, when in-kind revenue is large or relative to the total revenue and the the program expense ratio is usually high.
[14:52] It is worth understanding the valuation in the allocation methodology for the in-kind contribution before drawing conclusions from that kind of a ratio. Then, let's look at some of the areas that are rarely given attention, and that is the notes. The notes to the financial statements are the most unread section of an nonprofit's audited financials because, you know, they contain um a lot of information that matters for grantee capacity
[15:26] assessment. For example, the functional expense allocation note describes the methodology the organization used to split shared cost across programs, management, and fundraising functions. A note that say the organization allocated expenses on a basis of time and effort estimates and square footage, reviewed and approved annually by the management and the board, describes a methodologically sound process with appropriate oversight. Then, then there's also a note that
[15:59] says, "Expenses were allocated based on management estimates." It It provides essentially no information about the methodology and no basis for evaluating whether the resulting allocations are reasonable. So, it's worth paying attention to that note. The difference between these two notes is significant, and it correlates reliably with the overall quality of the organization's financial management. So, I would highly recommend that you don't ignore
[16:31] that note next time. Then, the other one is the liquidity note. This one discloses how the organization manages its liquidity and what financial resources are available to meet general expenditure within 12 months of the balance sheet date. This note often contains information about lines of credit, board-designated reserves, and the availability of donor-restricted funds for operational purposes that is not visible anywhere else in the financial statements.
[17:05] So, organizations that have thought carefully about liquidity management tend to write detailed, specific liquidity notes. And then, organizations that have that have not gone that far just give the generic disclosures that will not tell you much. So the significant accounting policies note is where revenue recognition grant accounting and its functional allocation methodologies are described. An organization that recognizes grant revenue when the conditions of the award
[17:39] are substantially met rather than when the cash is received is applying the more technical correct treatment. And then the an organization that only recognizes a grant revenue on receipt regardless of the conditions may be accelerating revenue recognition in ways that actually overstate the financial strength in any given year. And thankfully we have the GAAP, the IFRS for SMEs, and now the IMPAS that has outlined very detailed guidance on revenue recognition standards.
[18:14] The other one is the related party transactions. If disclosed, it tells you about the the governance environment. For example, transactions between organizations and board members, executives, or entities they control are not inherently problematic, but they do require proper disclosure and appropriate oversight. Organizations where related party transactions are common, large, and described with minimal detail, those ones warrant governance scrutiny.
[18:45] So when you read a grantee's financial statement with a portfolio lens, you're building a picture from multiple dimensions simultaneously. The balance sheet tells you about resilience and flexibility. The income statement tells you about revenue structure and concentration risk. The functional expense statement tells you about how the organization categorizes and manages its cost. The notes tell you about accounting policies, methodologies, choices, and the quality of financial
[19:18] governance. No single indicator is conclusive. A thin reserve position, for example, combined with excellent revenue diversification, a sophisticated allocation methodology, and a strong liquidity disclosure might represent a young organization that is well managed and growing. A robust reserve position combined with high revenue concentration, a vague allocation methodology, and a generic note disclosure may represent a mature organization whose financial management has kept pace
[19:52] with its growth. What you are looking for is pattern consistency. The quality of the allocation notes should be consistent with the quality of the audit opinion and the sophistication of the liquidity disclosures. When a financial package is internally inconsistent, when some parts of it suggest strong financial management and other parts suggest significant gaps, then that inconsistency in itself is a signal worth investigating before grant
[20:26] decision is made. The conversation you have with a grantee's finance team during due diligence is also a data point. How they describe their financial management processes, how quickly they can answer specific questions about the allocation methodology or their grant tracking systems, how they respond when you ask about a specific line item variance tells you something that no financial statement can tell you directly. The quality of that conversation is a proxy for the quality of the financial
[21:00] management systems underneath that organization. So, reading grantee financial statements with a portfolio perspective is a skill. It is built through practice and through knowing which questions to bring to the documents. The standard due diligence checklist that we know gives the program officers a starting point, but it was not designed in many cases to assess the specific questions that matters for most grant outcomes, whether this organization has the financial
[21:32] infrastructure to do what it's promising to do. In the next video this week, we go into the specific leading indicators, the financial signals that appear before problem surfaces in program delivery. These are the metrics and patterns that allow a grants portfolio director to intervene early and constructively rather than managing a crisis that were predictable 6 months earlier. If this raise questions about grantees in your current portfolio or about your
[22:05] organization's own financial statements, you can leave a comment. The most useful future content in this series will come from the specific challenges that you're actually navigat- navigating and sharing. Thank you for watching today, and this is the Farm Framework.
